wa_liberty_crack_free.belay: At a bolted station just below the Lithuanian Lip roof.
wa_liberty_crack_free.notes: Identical to the original Liberty Crack P1: a right-facing corner then splitter crack to a bolted belay below the Lithuanian Lip.

The Lithuanian Lip, free: fun 5.11- corner climbing leads to a scrunchy, powerful traverse to finger locks above the lip; lock in, high-step to the lip, and stick 5.12- moves to a small stance below the old bolt ladder. This is the pitch Brooke Sandahl first led on gear in 1991.

The modern free variation (Schaefer/Lee/Herrington/Hadley, 2016-17) that avoids the crumbling bolt ladder: move right, clip a higher bolt, cross sloping ledges, and mantel through cruxy foot moves past four protection bolts before rejoining the original line.
A thin crux move gains a small roof before the pitch rejoins the original Liberty Crack line below easier ground.
Jam a crack that hardens from 5.8 to 5.10, same as the original route's corresponding pitch, to a bolted belay.
A relatively relaxed corner pitch to another bolted belay.
Mostly easy stemming to a brief crux surmounting a big block past a single shiny bolt.

wa_liberty_crack_free.belay: On a small seat built from a couple of pitons and a cam or two.
wa_liberty_crack_free.notes: Steep moves off the belay to a ramp/corner with a long-runner bolt and an overlap move to a small seat.

wa_liberty_crack_free.belay: On a sheltered, tree-dotted triangular ledge, anchored in a finger crack.
wa_liberty_crack_free.notes: Fun quartz features and 5.6 chimneys lead to a triangular ledge with a finger-crack gear anchor.

wa_liberty_crack_free.belay: At a large tree, or alternatively off nearby crack placements.
wa_liberty_crack_free.notes: A long, excellent corner-and-slab pitch with airy East Face exposure, ending at a large tree belay.
Easy terrain leads to sandy ledges below the summit shoulder.

wa_liberty_crack_free.belay: At a bolted anchor in an alcove near the summit shoulder, where the descent gully starts.
wa_liberty_crack_free.notes: Easy simul-climbing/scrambling gains the bolted alcove near the summit shoulder, the top of the shared two-rappel descent into Beckey Gully.

wa_liberty_bell_independence_route.belay: On a ledge near a patch of yellow lichen and a pine tree.
wa_liberty_bell_independence_route.notes: Climbs the right edge of the East Face on horizontal breaks and cracks to a belay near a yellow lichen patch by a pine tree.
Crimp right then traverse left on a flake through a bolted section that follows the historic aid pendulum's line.

wa_liberty_bell_independence_route.belay: On a long ledge with a big horn, at a two-bolt anchor.
wa_liberty_bell_independence_route.notes: A left-facing quartz corner with a hard right-stemming sequence near two bolts.
Chimney/offwidth climbing for about 40 ft to a small alcove below the red 'Baer Ceiling,' an original aid pitch.

wa_liberty_bell_independence_route.belay: Just to the right of the Block Ceiling.
wa_liberty_bell_independence_route.notes: A ramp into a shallow corner with cruxy face moves protected by a fixed pin and copperheads; a mantle and slab move reach the belay. A sneaky, often-underrated crux.
A thin, piton-protected crack passes three stacked 'Cascade Ceilings' via a mantle move.
A technical rightward traverse into a shallow corner above a pine tree, with a reach-dependent boulder-problem section -- the original crux before the route's belays were repositioned.
Technical, classic granite stemming and jamming up an exposed corner beneath the 'Well Hung Ceiling' -- the route's overall crux pitch, matching its full free grade.

wa_liberty_bell_independence_route.belay: At the highest point of M&M Ledge, up and left of the previous stance.
wa_liberty_bell_independence_route.notes: Short pitch moving the belay left onto M&M Ledge, shared with Liberty Crack and Thin Red Line.

wa_liberty_bell_independence_route.belay: On a small terrace beneath an obvious splitter wide hand crack.
wa_liberty_bell_independence_route.notes: Chimney and blocky corner climbing past red roofs to the base of a splitter wide crack; an alternate left-trending ramp also exists.

wa_liberty_bell_independence_route.belay: At the bolted anchor on the clean slab beneath the Hercan Roofs.
wa_liberty_bell_independence_route.notes: A nice splitter 2-3 inch crack leads to a clean slab and bolted anchor beneath the Hercan Roofs.
A slab traverse up and right gains the ridge crest, followed by 3rd-class scrambling to the summit.

wa_castle_in_the_sky.belay: At a good belay at the left end of the ledge reached at the top of the slabs.
wa_castle_in_the_sky.notes: Start low in the moat below the buttress. Climb clean, well-protected granite slabs to a ledge, then follow it left to a good belay. If the cracks straight above the start are wet, the slab to their right is the alternative.

wa_castle_in_the_sky.belay: At an anchor in the next major crack or gully, up and right.
wa_castle_in_the_sky.notes: Take the gully on the left, not the steep option straight up. After about 50 ft, at a large ledge, turn right up a steep face of big jugs on solid rock with no protection. Trend up and right to the next major crack or gully for the anchor.

wa_castle_in_the_sky.belay: On an indistinct ledge at the top of the friable corners, with a fixed knifeblade in place.
wa_castle_in_the_sky.notes: Runout. Head up and left, then break right into the main corner system. A knifeblade piton protects the step right onto a slab. Friable, discontinuous corners lead to an indistinct ledge with a fixed #1 knifeblade at the belay. The big open-book corner above is steep, mossy and loose; do not take it.

wa_castle_in_the_sky.belay: At a stance beside some flakes at the end of the rising rightward traverse.
wa_castle_in_the_sky.notes: Head up and right. Avoid the obvious open-book corner and make a hard-to-spot step up and right onto the slab. A gentle rising traverse right includes about 25 ft of 5.10 face climbing on excellent rock. It ends at a stance by some flakes, where you belay.

wa_castle_in_the_sky.belay: At an uncomfortable stance in the right-hand crack past the roof, on a good #3 cam.
wa_castle_in_the_sky.notes: Up delicate flakes, then step right into a good crack as soon as possible. Well-protected crack climbing leads past a roof crux. Where the cracks fork, take the right one past a couple of vegetated moves to a cramped belay built around a good #3 cam placement.

wa_castle_in_the_sky.belay: On a heathery ledge beside the big gully, reached up the rib alongside it.
wa_castle_in_the_sky.notes: Continue up the crack to a rubble-covered ledge. A short, technical finger crack reaches an obvious ledge system. Traverse it right all the way to the huge gully, then run the rope up the rib beside the gully to a heather ledge belay.
Move into the huge gully, which is lined with solid, water-polished rock rather than rubble. Stem up it for a full rope length.

wa_castle_in_the_sky.belay: At an anchor below the steeper wall, just above the saddle on the ridge crest.
wa_castle_in_the_sky.notes: Continue up the polished gully to a saddle on the ridge crest. Scramble gravel and heather to an anchor at the base of the steeper wall above.
Climb compact rock up and right past gravel-covered ledges to an anchor. There is essentially no protection on this pitch.
Up the ridge crest. From here the good gneiss gives way to the compact, shattered rock typical of the Pickets. Gear is sparse.
Simul-climb the ridge to the notch below the west summit, on shattered rock with limited protection. Take care not to knock rock onto a partner below.
4th-class scrambling from the notch up to the west summit of Whatcom Peak.

co_childhood_s_end.belay: A two-bolt anchor on the right side of the buttress, at the foot of a short chimney.
co_childhood_s_end.notes: Begin a few metres right of the large boulder at the foot of the buttress. A low-angle crack with a tree in it crosses the face to a two-bolt station below a short chimney holding a 6-10 inch crack.
Climb the chimney (a #4 Camalot low, or a #2 higher), then the slab above past five bolts.

co_childhood_s_end.belay: A big sloping ledge reached after moving left across the water streak.
co_childhood_s_end.notes: Step right to a crack, climb it about 20 ft, then step left onto a slab with three bolts. A 5.11 variation steps sharply left past two bolts into a water groove and past one more bolt before rejoining the slab.
Clip a bolt out left, go around the corner, and climb the slab past two bolts. The last stretch to the anchor is run out.

co_childhood_s_end.belay: A ledge on the left with a two-bolt anchor, the best stance on the route and good for cutting rope drag.
co_childhood_s_end.notes: Clip the first bolt, climb right to the arete and past a couple of bolts, then make a long reach up and left to a ledge with a two-bolt anchor. Belaying here reduces rope drag.
Climb about 20 ft to the first bolt, traverse right about 15 ft to a hard-to-see bolt, and continue right over a ridge. The zig-zag line causes drag even with long draws.

The crux. Climb up to a finger crack and an undercling and clip a bolt, then move around onto the steep right side, underclinging past about 11 bolts before going straight up. It aids easily, and some think the hard section is best aided.
Long, sustained climbing past nine or ten bolts, with a hard move left into a groove worn by water, then the ground eases.
Slabs about 30 m up and left to a single bolt roughly 20 ft out left of the direct line, then up and right about 20 m to a new two-bolt anchor. Can be simul-climbed.
Continue up slab climbing past one bolt to a new two-bolt anchor.
No bolts and no gear. Ends at a large tree or the top of the cliff. Loose or damp lichen and snapping crystals demand focus.

wa_beyond_redlining.notes: Climbs the dark gray face above the two largest boulders at the tower's base, with multiple cruxes leading to a roof breached on the right side.
Navigate a bulge, ascend a rib, and traverse a steep slab; watch for loose rock in the approach gully below.
A more serious pitch than the grade suggests: polished rock, sparse bolts, and few positive holds on a left-trending ramp.
Low-angle terrain traversing above a large ledge to the belay.

wa_beyond_redlining.belay: On the large ledge system at the top of the featured vertical face.
wa_beyond_redlining.notes: Three fun cruxes lead to a featured, vertical finish on a large ledge system.
A steep face with a tricky bulge at an orange band; extend draws to manage rope drag. An unfinished, harder direct variant exists here but is not recommended as bolted.
A fun slab with easy runout, then steep athletic moves and a punchy crux at a bulge.

wa_beyond_redlining.belay: Just above the large roof, at the first anchor; the higher belay is uncomfortable.
wa_beyond_redlining.notes: A looming, very airy headwall with a wild corner past a couple of roofs.

wa_beyond_redlining.belay: A small stance reached by exiting left at the top of the overhanging face; skip the mid-face anchor, where a bolt spins.
wa_beyond_redlining.notes: Steeper than it looks: steep jugs, side-pulls, and jams on an overhanging face.
A golden, featured slab with a crux bulge, then an arête past a curious 'Mouth' feature.
A tricky boulder problem at the top of the pillar — the route's final and hardest crux — just below the summit shared with Mile High Club.

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.notes: Starts up a crack behind a short chimney block that becomes a left-facing corner, then works around a roof to the left; launched from a pedestal belay in the gully between Cathedral and 'The Monk'.

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.belay: At a small stance out right, after climbing behind and over the big chockstone.
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.notes: Navigate a steep chockstone — climbing behind and over it gives a bombproof terrain belay — then exit right into juggy cracks.
Stem and jam excellent twin finger cracks, mantle out of the corner system, step right to a short wide crack, then back onto twin finger cracks.

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.belay: At the left-hand end of the traverse that follows the quartz dike.
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.notes: Follows a quartz dike with a leftward traverse to the belay; discontinuous, juggy climbing with limited protection, so place gear smartly to manage rope drag.
Climb a right-facing corner to a cruxy mantle move, then ramble up ledges to a chimney on the right.

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.belay: At a tree growing on a ledge.
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.notes: A finger crack leads to an open book corner, then the climbing eases into 3rd-4th class terrain toward the headwall.

wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.belay: On nuts at the foot of the steep headwall.
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.notes: Easy, discontinuous terrain approaching the base of the headwall; many parties simul-climb this section to save time before the crux above.
A tricky move down low earns a solid medium cam before an obvious double-crack system up the start of the headwall; commonly linked with P9 into a single 55m 5.10a pitch.

Step rightward and choose between a wide crack or the harder, equally splitter finger crack further right (the more popular option); linked with P8 this becomes a sustained 55m 5.10a pitch and the technical crux of the route.
Two short, fun hand-crack steps separated by a ledge lead to 3rd class scrambling and the true summit.
wa_cathedral_peak_pasayten_se_buttress.anchor: Gear, then unroped 3rd class to the summit
